title: Sell-through rate: formula, benchmarks, and how to use it
summary: Sell-through rate is units sold over units received. With 15.8% of US retail sales returned in 2025, learn the formula, honest benchmarks, and how to act on it.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 10 November 2026.


Sell-through rate is the share of the stock you received that you have sold over a given period: units sold divided by units received, multiplied by 100. A range that received 1,000 units and sold 620 of them in its first eight weeks has a sell-through rate of 62% for that window.


The formula fits on a sticky note, which is exactly why it gets misread. The same product can show 9% sell-through after one week and 71% after a season, and both numbers are correct. Most guides then hand you a single benchmark, usually "80% is good," without saying which window, which category, or where the figure comes from.


This guide is for buyers, merchandise planners, and allocators who read sell-through every week to decide whether a product needs a reorder, a transfer, or a price step. It covers how to calculate the sell-through rate properly, why generic benchmarks fall apart, where the number misleads, and how to turn it into weekly decisions. If you want to see these readings on your own range, you can[review your sell-through with our planning team](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


**Key Takeaways**


- US retailers expected 15.8% of their 2025 sales to be returned (about $849.9 billion), and 19.3% of online sales, according to the NRF and Happy Returns. A sell-through rate built on gross sales overstates what really left the building.
- A Coresight Research survey of more than 200 senior US retail decision makers put 2018 markdown losses at $300 billion, or 12% of non-grocery sales, with 53% of unplanned markdown costs traced to inventory misjudgments.
- IHL Group estimates retail inventory distortion (overstocks plus out-of-stocks) at about $1.73 trillion a year, which is the gap a weekly sell-through reading is meant to catch early.
- The widely quoted "80% sell-through" target has no primary source and no stated time window. A target is only meaningful when it is tied to a period and built from your own comparable seasons.


## What is sell-through rate?


Sell-through rate is the percentage of inventory received from suppliers that a retailer sells to customers within a defined period. It is calculated as units sold divided by units received, multiplied by 100, and it is usually tracked by product, variant, store, and week to judge whether demand matches the quantity bought.


Three choices sit behind every sell-through number, and two teams can disagree simply because they made different ones.


**Units or value.** Unit sell-through answers "how much of what we bought has gone?" Value sell-through (sales at cost divided by receipts at cost) weights expensive items more heavily. Buyers mostly work in units; finance often prefers value. Pick one per report and label it.


**Total or full-price.** Total sell-through counts every unit sold, discounted or not. Full-price sell-through counts only units sold at the original ticket price. A range can hit 85% total sell-through and still be a poor buy if half of it went at 40% off, so full-price sell-through is the figure that tells you whether the original buy was right.


**Received or available.** The classic formula divides by units received. Some teams divide by beginning-of-period stock instead, which suits replenished basics better than one-shot seasonal buys. Both are valid, but they cannot be compared with each other.


## How to calculate sell-through rate


The sell-through rate formula is:


**Sell-through rate = units sold in the period / units received in the period x 100**


For a seasonal buy, "received" is usually the cumulative quantity delivered to date, and "sold" is cumulative units sold since launch. For a replenished product, use units sold in the period divided by opening stock plus receipts in the period.


### Worked example (illustrative)


The figures below are invented to show the arithmetic.


A footwear retailer buys 2,400 pairs of a waterproof hiking boot for the autumn season, delivered in two drops: 1,600 pairs in week 1 and 800 pairs in week 5.


WeekCumulative receivedCumulative soldSell-through ratePlan11,6001509.4%8%21,60029018.1%16%41,60052032.5%30%52,40064026.7%30%82,4001,03042.9%48%


Two things stand out. The dip in week 5 comes from the second drop landing and the denominator jumping, while demand held steady. And by week 8 the boot is five points behind plan, which on 2,400 pairs is about 120 pairs of unsold stock relative to plan, enough to act on while there are still ten weeks of selling left.


**Pro Tip:** Plot cumulative sell-through against a plan curve, never a single end-of-season target. A product at 43% in week 8 against a 48% curve is a reallocation candidate today; the same product compared with an "80% by end of season" target looks fine until it is too late.


Elena, the boot buyer in this example, used to review sell-through monthly. Switching to a weekly curve per variant showed that the week-8 shortfall sat almost entirely in two half sizes in southern stores, where an early warm spell had slowed demand, while northern stores were close to selling out of the core sizes. She moved 90 pairs north instead of planning a markdown. (Elena is an illustrative example.)


## What is a good sell-through rate?


There is no single good sell-through rate, because the number depends on the window you measure and the type of product. Glossary pages commonly quote 80% as strong, or a "healthy" range of 40% to 80%, and some add category tables (apparel around 60% to 70%, perishables above 90%). None of these ranges traces back to a published study, and at least one page that repeats them describes them as convention rather than measured data. They make a reasonable conversation starter and a poor target.


The window changes everything:


Measurement windowWhat it tells youHow to set the targetWeek 1 to 2 after launchEarly read on demand versus the buyFrom the first weeks of comparable past launchesWeekly, in seasonWhether the product is on its curveCumulative plan curve per product or familyEnd of full-price periodQuality of the original buyShare of units your margin plan assumed at full priceEnd of season (all prices)How much stock is left to carry or clearLeftover stock your clearance channels can absorbRolling 4 or 13 weeks (basics)Whether replenishment depth is rightWeeks of cover target, not a percentage


Category matters as much as the window. A fragrance gift set built for December should be close to sold through by early January. A jewelry core line or a furniture range may sell steadily over a year or more, and a low sell-through rate after eight weeks says nothing alarming about it.


The practical answer is to build your own target curve from your last two or three comparable seasons for each product family, then judge each product against that curve. One mistake we repeatedly see is a single company-wide sell-through target applied to fast seasonal ranges and slow core ranges alike, which flags the wrong products every week.


## Where sell-through readings mislead


A sell-through rate is only as good as the data behind it, and most misreadings come from structure rather than effort: the inputs sit in different systems, and the averages hide what matters.


**Returns.** If sales are counted gross, a range with high returns looks better than it is. According to the[NRF and Happy Returns 2025 Retail Returns Landscape](https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/consumers-expected-to-return-nearly-850-billion-in-merchandise-in-2025) , US retailers expected 15.8% of annual sales to be returned in 2025, and 19.3% of online sales. For categories sold mostly online, calculate sell-through on net units (sold minus returned) or the number will drift up and then fall back weeks later.


**Stockouts.** A product that sold out in half its stores in week 3 shows a modest sell-through rate, but demand was capped by availability, not interest. Sell-through measures what sold from what you had, not what customers wanted. Flag weeks with zero stock so a strong product is not mistaken for an average one.


**Averages across sizes and stores.** A range at 55% can hide 80% in the core sizes and 25% at the edges of the size curve, or 75% in city stores and 35% in out-of-town ones. The average suggests no action; the detail suggests a transfer and a smaller edge-size buy next season.


**Receipts timing.** As the boot example shows, a late drop pushes sell-through down without any change in demand. Read the curve alongside receipts, or compare sell-through only between dates when nothing new arrived.


The merchandise planners we work with often underestimate how much of a "bad" sell-through rate is really an allocation problem. Across Metreecs' work with multi-store retailers, a range that looks weak at company level frequently has enough demand in total; it simply sits in the wrong stores.


## How to use sell-through rate for buying and markdown decisions


The sell-through rate earns its place when every reading maps to an action. A simple grid compares each product's cumulative sell-through with its plan curve and with its stock position.


Sell-through versus planStock positionTypical actionWell aheadLow cover in most locationsReorder if lead time allows, protect full priceAhead in some locations, behind in othersUnevenTransfer stock between stores or to the web shopSlightly behindNormalWatch one more week, check visual merchandising and availabilityClearly behind, early in seasonHigh coverRebalance first, then a shallow, targeted price stepClearly behind, late in seasonHigh coverPlan clearance depth and channel; cut the next buy


**Reorder.** A product ahead of its curve in week 3 or 4 is the strongest reorder signal you will get, but only if a supplier can deliver inside the season. Keeping part of the budget open for in-season buys is what turns a strong sell-through reading into extra full-price sales. Our guide on[allocating stock to maximize full-price sales](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/smarter-stock-allocation-to-maximize-full-price-sales) covers how to split the initial buy.


**Reallocate.** An uneven sell-through rate across stores is the cheapest problem to fix, because the stock already exists. Moving units from slow to fast locations raises the total sell-through rate without a price cut. Our article on[rebalancing stock between stores](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/rebalancing-allocation-stores) walks through when a transfer pays for itself.


**Mark down.** When a product is behind everywhere, an early, shallow markdown on the slow variants sells against more remaining weeks of demand than a deep cut at the end. The Coresight Research survey found that 53% of unplanned markdown costs came from inventory misjudgments, which is a reminder that the markdown decision usually starts with the buy.


**Next buy.** End-of-season sell-through by size, color, and store cluster is the best input for next season's depth. A variant that finished at 30% full-price sell-through two seasons running needs a smaller buy, not a better markdown plan.


Priya plans home textiles for a 30-store retailer. Her linen bedding sold through at 64% by week 6, comfortably ahead of a 55% curve, while the matching cushions sat at 31%. Instead of discounting the cushions across the chain, she moved them to the 12 stores where the bedding was selling best and paired them on the bed displays. The cushions caught up to 49% within four weeks, and she cut their depth for the following season. (Priya is an illustrative example.)


**Statistic callout:** US non-grocery retailers lost $300 billion to markdowns in 2018, equal to 12% of their sales, per a Coresight Research survey of more than 200 senior retail decision makers.


## Sell-through rate vs inventory turnover and other metrics


Sell-through is often confused with inventory turnover, but they answer different questions.


MetricFormula (simplified)Question it answersBest forSell-through rateUnits sold / units received x 100How much of what we bought has sold?Seasonal buys, launches, markdown timingInventory turnoverCost of goods sold / average inventory at costHow many times did stock turn over in the year?Replenished ranges, financial reportingWeeks of coverStock on hand / average weekly salesHow long will current stock last?Replenishment and transfersFull-price sell-throughUnits sold at full price / units received x 100How much of the buy earned full margin?Judging the original buy


A high inventory turnover with a low full-price sell-through usually means stock is moving, but at a discount. A high sell-through rate with frequent stockouts usually means the buy was too shallow. Reading two metrics together tells you which way to adjust.


Reading these metrics at product and location level every week is where forecasting matters most. When demand is forecast for each product in each store, the plan curve itself becomes more accurate, and a gap between actual and planned sell-through is far more likely to point to a real decision. That is the logic behind[product-level inventory optimization](https://www.metreecs.com/inventory-optimization) .


## FAQ


### How do you calculate sell-through rate?


Divide the number of units sold in a period by the number of units received in the same period, then multiply by 100. For a seasonal buy, use cumulative units sold since launch over cumulative units received to date. For replenished basics, divide sales by opening stock plus receipts in the period.


### What is a good sell-through rate for retail?


It depends on the window and the product. The 80% figure quoted online has no primary source and rarely states a period. Build a target curve from your own comparable seasons and judge each product against where it should be in that week, not against a single end-of-season number.


### Is a 100% sell-through rate good?


Not necessarily. Selling out completely often means you bought too little and lost sales once the shelf was empty. A product that sells out early in most stores is usually a signal to buy deeper or reorder sooner next time.


### What is the difference between sell-through and inventory turnover?


Sell-through measures the share of received stock that has sold, so it suits one-time seasonal buys. Inventory turnover measures how many times average stock is sold and replaced over a year, so it suits replenished ranges and financial reporting.


### How often should you track sell-through rate?


Weekly for seasonal, fashion-driven, and newly launched products, because the window to reorder or transfer closes within weeks. Monthly or on a rolling 13-week basis works for stable basics, where weeks of cover is often the more useful measure.


## Conclusion


Sell-through rate is a simple ratio that becomes useful only when it is tied to a time window, read at product and store level, and compared with a plan curve you built from your own seasons. Start by setting weekly curves for your next seasonal range and agreeing which action each gap triggers.
